content: The sense of taste is a critical component of an individual's overall health. It plays a vital role in the enjoyment of food, which is essential for proper nutrition. Any disruption in taste perception can negatively impact a person's quality of life by affecting their appetite, body weight, and psychological well-being. Various treatment approaches have been used to address taste disturbances, but there is no consensus on the most effective intervention. This Cochrane Review was conducted to evaluate the effects of different interventions for managing taste disturbances. It is an update of a previous review first published in November 2014. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of interventions for managing taste disturbances in affected patients. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including Cochrane Oral Health's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and AMED, up to July 4, 2017. Additional searches were performed in ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Abstracts from scientific meetings and conferences were also reviewed. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date during the search. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions with control interventions. Cross-over trials were also included. Two pairs of reviewers independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Adverse events reported in the trials were also collected. A total of 10 trials involving 581 participants were included in the review, with nine trials (566 participants) included in the quantitative analyses. Three trials (30%) were assessed as having a low risk of bias, four trials (40%) had a high risk of bias, and three trials (30%) had an unclear risk of bias. The review focused on taste disorders that were idiopathic, or caused by zinc deficiency or chronic renal failure. Nine trials, involving 544 participants, compared zinc supplementation with placebo for managing taste disorders. Two of these trials included children and adolescents with mean ages of 10 and 11.2 years, while the remaining seven trials involved adult participants. Two trials assessed patient-reported outcomes for improvement in taste acuity with zinc supplementation, but the evidence was of very low quality (risk ratio [RR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.94 to 2.09; 119 participants). Objective outcomes for taste acuity improvement in idiopathic and zinc-deficient taste disorder patients were meta-analyzed, showing a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.44 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.65; 366 participants, three trials), but the evidence was also of very low quality. One cross-over trial was analyzed separately for taste detection and taste recognition, using the first half of the results. The mean difference (MD) for taste detection was 2.50 (95% CI 0.93 to 4.07; 14 participants), and for taste recognition, it was 3.00 (95% CI 0.66 to 5.34; 14 participants). Both outcomes were based on very low-quality evidence. Another meta-analysis of taste acuity improvement using dichotomous data in idiopathic and zinc-deficient taste disorder patients showed an RR of 1.42 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.84; 292 participants, two trials), but again, the evidence was of very low quality. Adverse events were reported in four of the nine trials using zinc supplementation. These included eczema, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, decreased blood iron levels, increased blood alkaline phosphatase levels, and minor increases in blood triglycerides. One trial evaluated the use of acupuncture for taste discrimination, reporting a mean difference of 2.80 (95% CI -1.18 to 6.78; 37 participants), but the evidence was of very low quality. No adverse events were reported in the acupuncture trial. None of the included trials provided data that could be meta-analyzed for health-related quality of life in patients with taste disorders. The authors concluded that the evidence for the effectiveness of zinc supplements in improving taste acuity, as reported by patients, is of very low quality and insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Similarly, the evidence for zinc supplements improving taste acuity in patients with zinc deficiency or idiopathic taste disorders is also of very low quality. There was no evidence to support the role of zinc supplements in improving taste discrimination or addressing health-related quality of life in patients with taste disorders. The evidence for acupuncture in improving taste discrimination in cases of idiopathic dysgeusia (distorted taste) and hypogeusia (reduced ability to taste) was also of very low quality and insufficient to draw conclusions. No trials directly compared zinc supplementation with acupuncture, so no conclusions could be made regarding the superiority of one intervention over the other.
